chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 106 — The Birth and Calling of Noah
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest primary-language witnesses responsibly available for this chapter. The fragmentary Aramaic text of 4Q204 (4QEnochᶜ ar), fragment 5 columns i–ii, governs its extant wording in verses 1–2 and 13–19. The fourth-century Chester Beatty–Michigan Papyrus XII supplies the continuous Greek text of Chapter 106 where Aramaic is absent or broken. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann’s 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, printed pages 90–92, fills remaining physical lacunae and confirms the complete nineteen-verse sequence. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, no commentary was used as Scripture, and no text absent from these primary witnesses was supplied.

verses.text: After some days, my son Methuselah took a wife for his son Lamech. She conceived by him and gave birth to a son.
verses.study: The narrative moves from Enoch’s heavenly instruction into his family line. The child’s human descent is stated before his extraordinary appearance raises questions about it.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:25–29 — Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah stand in one recorded family line
Luke 3:36–37 — Noah’s ancestry is traced through Lamech and Methuselah

verses.text: His body was white as snow and red like the flower of a rose. The hair of his head was white like pure wool, thick and splendid, and his eyes were beautiful. When he opened his eyes, he lit up the whole house like the sun, and the entire house became exceedingly bright.
verses.study: Noah’s appearance is described with images of purity, vitality, and heavenly brightness. The signs provoke wonder but do not themselves answer who he is.
crossReferences: Daniel 7:9 — white garments and wool-like hair accompany heavenly splendor
Matthew 17:2 — radiant light makes hidden glory visible

verses.text: When he rose from the midwife’s hands, he opened his mouth and spoke to the Lord of righteousness.
verses.study: The newborn’s first act is directed toward the righteous Lord. His remarkable speech is worshipful rather than self-exalting.
crossReferences: Psalm 8:2 — praise is established from the mouths of infants
Luke 1:64 — a newly opened mouth immediately blesses God

verses.text: His father Lamech was afraid of him, fled, and went to his father Methuselah.
verses.study: Lamech responds to what he cannot explain with fear and flight. He seeks the discernment of the previous generation rather than settling the matter himself.
crossReferences: Genesis 28:16–17 — an unexpected encounter with the holy produces fear
Luke 1:12–13 — extraordinary divine signs initially cause fear

verses.text: He said to him, ‘I have fathered an unusual son. He is not like a human being but resembles the children of heaven’s angels; his nature is different and he is not like us. His eyes are like rays of the sun, and his face is glorious.
verses.study: Lamech accurately reports what he sees but draws an uncertain inference from appearance. The narrative allows the question to sharpen before Enoch gives the interpretation.
crossReferences: Judges 13:6 — an awesome appearance leads a witness to compare a messenger with an angel
Daniel 10:6 — eyes and face are described with fiery and radiant imagery

verses.text: It seems to me that he did not come from me but from the angels, and I fear that something extraordinary may happen on the earth in his days.
verses.study: Fear converts resemblance into doubt about fatherhood. Lamech nevertheless senses correctly that the child’s days will coincide with an earth-changing event.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:1–4 — angelic transgression forms the troubling background to Lamech’s fear
Luke 1:65–66 — an extraordinary birth prompts questions about the child’s future

verses.text: Now, my father, I beg and implore you to go to our father Enoch and learn the truth from him, for his dwelling is with the angels.’
verses.study: Lamech does not ask for speculation but for truth from one granted heavenly knowledge. Methuselah becomes the messenger between generations.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:24 — Enoch’s exceptional walk with God sets him apart
Malachi 2:7 — reliable instruction is sought from one entrusted with knowledge

verses.text: When Methuselah heard his son’s words, he came to me at the ends of the earth, for he had heard that I was there. He cried aloud; I heard his voice, came to him, and said, ‘Here I am, my son. Why have you come to me?’
verses.study: The distant Enoch remains responsive to his son’s cry. The movement toward the ends of the earth underscores the urgency of securing a trustworthy answer.
crossReferences: Genesis 22:7 — ‘Here I am, my son’ expresses attentive family response
Psalm 61:2 — a cry goes up from the end of the earth

verses.text: He answered me, ‘I have come to you because of a grave matter and because of a disturbing sight that has drawn me here.
verses.study: Methuselah frames the report as both a family crisis and a sign requiring interpretation. He brings anxiety into the open before Enoch.
crossReferences: Daniel 7:15–16 — a troubling vision leads to a request for its truth
Habakkuk 1:2–3 — distressing sights are brought before one who can answer

verses.text: Now, my father, hear me. A son has been born to my son Lamech whose likeness and nature are not like those of human beings. His body is whiter than snow and redder than a rose’s flower; the hair of his head is whiter than pure wool, and his eyes are like rays of the sun. When he opened them, he lit up the whole house.
verses.study: Methuselah carefully repeats the observed details rather than embellishing the conclusion. Faithful testimony provides the basis for discernment.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 19:15 — a matter is established through careful testimony
Luke 2:17–19 — witnesses report what they saw and heard concerning an extraordinary child

verses.text: He rose from the midwife’s hands, opened his mouth, and blessed the Lord of heaven.
verses.study: The repetition clarifies the newborn’s speech as blessing. Noah’s first recorded orientation is toward the Lord of heaven.
crossReferences: Psalm 34:1 — blessing the Lord becomes the speaker’s first and continual response
Luke 1:68 — inspired speech opens with blessing the Lord

verses.text: His father Lamech was afraid and fled to me. He does not believe that the child came from him but thinks he resembles heaven’s angels. So I have come to you that you may make the truth known to me.’
verses.study: The question reaches Enoch without disguising Lamech’s doubt. Truth is needed to restore both family identity and understanding of the sign.
crossReferences: Proverbs 18:13 — a matter should be heard before judgment is given
John 8:32 — known truth brings freedom from false conclusions

verses.text: Then I, Enoch, answered him, ‘The Lord will bring something new upon the earth. I know this, for I have seen it in a vision and have already shown you that in the days of my father Jared some from heaven transgressed the word of the Lord.
verses.study: Enoch links Noah’s birth to earlier revelation about the Watchers. The new event will answer a transgression already known in the family’s remembered history.
crossReferences: 1 Enoch 6:1–8 — the Watchers bind themselves to descend and transgress
Isaiah 43:19 — God announces a new act that must be perceived

verses.text: They sinned, transgressed the appointed order, joined themselves to women, committed sin with them, took some of them as wives, and fathered children by them.
verses.study: The crisis is traced to a deliberate crossing of divine boundaries. Desire becomes union, and union produces violent consequences on earth.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:1–4 — heavenly beings take women and produce mighty offspring
Jude 6–7 — beings who abandon their proper place are linked with sexual transgression

verses.text: Their offspring on the earth will be giants, born not according to spirit but according to flesh. A great punishment will come upon the earth, and the earth will be washed clean from all corruption.
verses.study: The hybrid violence belongs to corruptible flesh and brings comprehensive punishment. The coming washing is both destruction and the removal of corruption.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:4–7 — giants, pervasive evil, and announced destruction appear together
1 Peter 3:20–21 — floodwater becomes a pattern of cleansing and salvation

verses.text: A great destruction will come over the whole earth: there will be floodwaters and a vast destruction for one year.
verses.study: The judgment is worldwide in scope and bounded within an announced season. The warning interprets the coming flood before it arrives.
crossReferences: Genesis 7:10–24 — floodwaters overwhelm the earth
2 Peter 3:5–6 — the ancient world perishes through water

verses.text: But this child born to you will remain upon the earth, and his three sons will be saved with him. When all the people upon the earth die, he and his sons will be saved.
verses.study: Judgment does not erase the human family. Noah and his three sons become the preserved remnant through whom life continues.
crossReferences: Genesis 7:13, 23 — Noah and his family alone remain through the flood
Hebrews 11:7 — Noah’s faithful action saves his household

verses.text: Now tell your son Lamech that the child born to him is truly his son. Call his name Noah, for he will remain for you; he and his sons will be saved from the destruction that will come upon the earth because of all the sin and lawlessness completed upon it in his days.
verses.study: Enoch directly resolves Lamech’s fear: Noah is truly his son. His name is joined to survival and rest amid the consequences of completed lawlessness.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:28–29 — Lamech names Noah in hope of relief
Genesis 8:18–22 — Noah’s preserved family emerges after the destruction

verses.text: Afterward, lawlessness will arise even more greatly than the lawlessness completed on earth before, for I know the mysteries of the holy ones. The Lord has shown and taught me, and I have read in the heavenly tablets that generation after generation will grow worse until generations of truth arise. Then evil and lawlessness will end, violence will vanish from the earth, and good will come upon them.’
verses.study: The flood restrains one age of violence but does not perfect later humanity. Enoch’s heavenly record carries hope beyond recurring evil to generations in which truth and good finally prevail.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:21 — evil remains in the human heart after the flood
Isaiah 11:9 — violence gives way when the earth is filled with divine knowledge

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 106 begins the birth narrative of Noah. His radiant appearance and precocious blessing of the Lord terrify Lamech, who mistakes resemblance to heavenly beings for angelic paternity. The story treats fear seriously but resolves it through truthful revelation: Noah is genuinely Lamech’s son.

The family seeks understanding across four generations. Lamech goes to Methuselah, Methuselah journeys to Enoch, and Enoch answers from revelation previously received. Careful repetition matters in this chain; the witnesses report what happened so that interpretation rests on testimony rather than rumor.

Enoch places Noah’s birth within the crisis created by the Watchers. Their violation of the appointed order produced corrupting violence, and the flood will wash the earth clean. Noah’s unusual radiance therefore signals not that he shares the Watchers’ transgression but that he and his sons will be preserved through its judgment.

The heavenly tablets look beyond the flood as well. Later lawlessness will again grow, so one cleansing event does not remove every future human wrong. Yet the record also promises generations of truth in which evil, lawlessness, and violence end. Noah’s preservation is one stage in a longer divine purpose moving toward truth and good.

crossReferences: 1 Enoch 6:1–11:2 — the Watchers’ transgression leads to flood judgment and Noah’s preservation
1 Enoch 107:1–3 — Enoch completes the message and Methuselah names Noah
Genesis 5:25–32 — the lineage from Methuselah to Noah and his naming
Genesis 6:1–13 — angelic transgression, giants, corruption, and Noah’s favor
Genesis 7:11–24 — flood judgment leaves Noah’s household alive
Genesis 8:15–22 — the preserved family begins life upon the cleansed earth
Isaiah 54:9–10 — the waters of Noah frame a promise of enduring mercy
Matthew 24:37–39 — Noah’s days become a pattern of unexpected judgment
Hebrews 11:7 — Noah acts in faith and preserves his household
1 Peter 3:18–22 — Noah’s salvation through water is read as a pattern of deliverance
